title: Type annotations, inference, and explicit typing
hook: You can tell TypeScript the type of a value with an annotation, or let the compiler infer it from context. Good TypeScript code uses inference by default and adds explicit types where they clarify public APIs or catch bugs — similar to when C# uses var versus writing int explicitly.

blocks.text: Type annotations attach types to variables, parameters, and return positions: let count: number = 0. Type inference lets tsc deduce types when you omit annotations: const count = 0 infers number. Explicit typing is required when inference would be too wide (any), when defining public library exports, or when you want a narrower type than inference provides. Annotations are compile-time only — they erase on emit, unlike C# where int x is enforced by the CLR at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Syntax that declares the expected type of a value, written after a colon.
The compiler deducing a type from an initializer or return expression.
When inference chooses a broader type than you might expect, e.g. string instead of a literal.
entries.example: let status = 'pending'; // string, not 'pending' unless const or annotation

blocks.text: Over-annotating clutters code; under-annotating lets any leak through function boundaries. Senior style: annotate function signatures and exported APIs; let locals infer. C# developers often over-annotate every variable — in TypeScript, const message = 'ok' is preferred over const message: string = 'ok' unless widening is a problem. Inference powers editor autocomplete without repeating yourself.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.body: Annotate parameters and return types on exported functions. Let const and well-typed initializers infer. Use satisfies when you want checking without widening the inferred type.

items.title: Function boundaries
items.body: Public APIs: annotate parameters and returns so callers get contracts in .d.ts files.

items.title: Empty collections
items.body: const items: Order[] = []; — inference gives never[] without a hint.

items.title: Destructuring parameters
items.body: function load({ url }: { url: string }) — inline object types clarify shape.

items.title: Prefer inference for locals
items.body: const total = price * qty — tsc knows the math type; no need for : number.

diagram.title: Inference vs explicit annotation
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Source code] --> B{Annotation present?}
  B -->|yes| C[Use annotated type]
  B -->|no| D[Infer from initializer]
  D --> E{Contextual typing?}
  E -->|yes| F[Parameter/return context]
  E -->|no| G[Best common type]
  C --> H[Type checker]
  F --> H
  G --> H
  H --> I[Emit JS — types erased]

snippet.label: Explicit function signature
snippet.explanation: Export boundaries deserve explicit types. C# public methods always declare return types; same discipline applies here for libraries.

snippet.label: Inference from const
snippet.explanation: Object literal inference gives readable types without annotations. Use satisfies Config for validation while keeping precise keys.

snippet.label: Widening with let vs const
snippet.explanation: let widens string literals to string. Union annotations preserve allowed states — similar to C# enum or discriminated states, but erased at run time.

snippet.label: Contextual typing in callbacks
snippet.explanation: Contextual typing infers parameter types from the expected function type — you often skip annotating callback parameters when the outer type is explicit.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Annotating every local with redundant types. Using any instead of unknown at boundaries. Writing : object when you mean a specific shape. Relying on implicit any (disabled under strict) by leaving parameters untyped.

blocks.text: Return type annotations can widen or narrow what inference would pick — explicit return types on exported APIs prevent implementation details from leaking into the public type. satisfies (TS 4.9+) checks against a type without changing inference — useful for config objects. noImplicitAny and noImplicitReturns are strict flags interviewers expect you to know. For generic functions, annotations on type parameters (<T extends string>) document constraints. Unlike C#, you cannot overload on return type alone for inference tricks — use function overload signatures instead (module 04).

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Lies at run time — rejected in review

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using any on external input. Not knowing difference between type annotation and assertion (as). Saying annotations affect run-time performance. Unable to explain when never[] appears.

interviewTakeaways: Annotate public function signatures; let well-initialized locals infer.
const narrows literals; let widens to string/number/boolean.
unknown at boundaries, then narrow — never trust JSON.parse annotations alone.
60s: Annotations are compile-time contracts that erase. Inference from const and context reduces noise. Export explicit types for API stability. C# enforces at runtime; TS does not.
Follow-up: when would you use satisfies instead of a type annotation?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'I type everything explicitly.' Strong: 'Infer locals, annotate exports, unknown at boundaries.'
const items = [] infers never[] — need Order[] annotation or push hint.
Strong answer: 'Inference default, explicit at API edges, satisfies for config, no any on input.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript files can be type-checked via JSDoc annotations — same erasure model without .ts extension.
C# var still has compile-time and runtime types. TS inference is compile-time only and erases.
